title: Tesla's Missing Autopilot Data Showed It Detected A Hazard Before Fatal Crash, Despite Claims It Was Missing

reading.body:
Tesla told a grieving family after a fatal Autopilot crash that crash data from the vehicle was unavailable. A hacker demonstrated that the data existed on the vehicle, contradicting Tesla's statement. A jury found Tesla partially responsible for the crash and a judge upheld a verdict ordering the company to pay damages.

This is a failure of transparency in a deployed autonomous system. The failure occurred at the point of communicating with the public about what information the system had recorded. It would have been caught by checking whether data was actually irretrievable before making claims about its absence to crash victims.

It is not established from these reports whether Tesla's initial claim was made in error or with intent to mislead.

summary:
# Summary

A lawsuit against Tesla concluded after a fatal crash in March 2024 killed Naibel Benavides Leon and seriously injured Dillon Angulo when a self-driving Tesla struck their parked vehicle. A jury found Tesla partially responsible in August 2025, and a judge upheld the verdict in February 2026, ordering the company to pay 243 million dollars in damages. Tesla had claimed it lacked crash data from the vehicle, but a Russian hacker working through Tesla's bug bounty program recovered the data and proved the company actually possessed it, contradicting Tesla's statement to the grieving family.

This disclosure became crucial evidence in the case as Elon Musk prepares to launch fully autonomous Cybercabs. The incident raises concerns about Tesla's transparency regarding self-driving safety, particularly since Teslas with active driver-assist systems were involved in 207 crashes in May, a record high. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is investigating potential self-driving software failures, suggesting questions remain about the safety readiness of fully autonomous vehicles before their market release.
